explanation.text: RFC 9110, published in June 2022, is the HTTP standard that classifies request methods, including PUT, as idempotent.
Section 9.2.2 of RFC 9110 explicitly states that PUT, DELETE, and safe request methods are idempotent.
RFC 9110 was published as an Internet Standard in June 2022, establishing it as the definitive HTTP standard at that time.

excerpts.text: This document updates RFC 3864 and obsoletes RFCs 2818, 7231, 7232, 7233, 7235, 7538, 7615, 7694, and portions of 7230.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-abstract-2)
Copyright (c) 2022 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors.

This revision of HTTP separates the definition of semantics (this document) and caching ([[CACHING](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#CACHING)]) from the current HTTP/1.1 messaging syntax ([[HTTP/1.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#HTTP11)]) to allow each major protocol version to progress independently while referring to the same core semantics.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.2-5)

HTTP semantics include the intentions defined by each request method ([Section 9](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#methods)), extensions to those semantics that might be described in request header fields, status codes that describe the response ([Section 15](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#status.codes)), and other control data and resource metadata that might be given in response fields.[¶](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9110/#section-1.3-3)

excerpts.text: PUT is idempotent and POST is not.

RFC 9110, section 9.2.2, calls a method idempotent when the intended effect of several identical requests equals the effect of one. PUT, DELETE and the safe methods qualify; POST is not idempotent as defined, though a single resource may implement it that way.
| Idempotent | Yes | No, as the method is registered |
A method is idempotent when the intended effect of several identical requests is the same as the effect of one (RFC 9110, section 9.2.2). The standard names PUT, DELETE and the safe methods.

assessment.rationale: The source cites RFC 9110 §9.2.2, which defines PUT as idempotent, and explicitly states that PUT is not safe but is idempotent. Span 42 in the table confirms PUT as idempotent. RFC 9110 was published in June 2022, aligning with the claimed timeframe.

assessment.provenance_note: RFC 9110 is cited as the source of the classification.

excerpts.text: PUT is not safe (it changes stuff) but it is idempotent (doing the same PUT ten times leaves you in the same state as doing it once).

assessment.rationale: Span 17 states that HTTP defines PUT as idempotent according to RFC 9110, section 9.2.2. Span 100 cites RFC 9110 (June 2022) as a source, confirming the standard's existence and timeframe.
assessment.provenance_note: RFC 9110 is cited as the authoritative source for the HTTP standard in June 2022.

excerpts.text: HTTP defines `GET`, `HEAD`, `PUT` and `DELETE` as idempotent: sending the same request twice has the same effect as sending it once ([RFC 9110, section 9.2.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2)). `POST` and `PATCH` are not. “Create a payment” twice creates two payments.

Sources: [IETF, “The Idempotency-Key HTTP Header Field”, draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07 (Oct 15, 2025)](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07.html); [RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics, section 9.2.2 (June 2022)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2); [Stripe API reference, “Idempotent requests”](https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests)
